newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialist congress debates new premier.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialist congress debates new premier.

text.p: A congress of Bulgaria's ruling Socialists held closed-door talks overnight to select a new prime minister and party leader after Zhan Videnov's surprise resignation on Saturday.

Delegates said half a dozen names had been proposed, including Videnov, U.S.-born former foreign minister Georgi Pirinski and leading party reformists, and it was not yet clear whether the two posts would be split.
Voting was not expected before early Monday.
On Sunday, the congress rejected a package of seven resolutions signed by 153 party reformists, raising Videnov's chances of retaining his post.
The resolutions included statements on economic reform, media policy, the ex-communist party's commitment to social democracy, and relations with other political parties.

Delegates used to communist-style congresses approved them automatically, but then Videnov observed that one resolution implied the separation of the posts of party leader and prime minister, which he opposes, and insisted they be voted again.
Nikolai Kamov, head of parliament's foreign policy committee, said the leadership issue was preventing the congress from considering anything else.
"The party is dead," he said. "They refused to amend the statutes and adopt a programme just because of one person."

The 37-year-old premier stunned delegates by announcing at Saturday's opening session that he felt he lacked the necessary support to continue as premier and party leader and had submitted his resignation to parliament.

Critics dismissed the move as a ploy to prove he had the support of his party, observing that parliament was in recess and speaker Blagovest Sendov was in Israel. Sendov returned on Sunday evening and said he would decide on Monday whether an extraordinary session was necessary.

"This decision should have been taken 40 days ago when it became evident that there was no confidence in the government," said Pirinski, who resigned last month after a party confidence vote gave Videnov only narrow backing.

Pirinski told the congress he had quit because Videnov's government did not have sufficient public support to implement a tough monetary regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund as a last-ditch attempt to halt economic collapse.
Delegates painted a bleak picture of the country's crisis and called for a genuine commitment to reform and concrete measures to fight corruption.

Videnov became prime minister after parliamentary elections in December 1994. Criticism of his government, which is half-way through its four-year term, became more vocal after the Socialists' defeat in last month's presidential election.
The government's failure to meet reform targets including closing or restructuring loss-making state enterprises has led to the suspension of funding from the World Bank and IMF.

The government has not yet finalised the 1997 budget. Videnov has accepted an IMF proposal for a currency board fixed exchange rate mechanism, expected to be set up early next year to restore confidence and halt the slide in the lev.
